section.title: Fools, Sluggards, and Gossips
section.sectionRationale: Part of the Hezekiah collection, 25:1 to 29:27, this chapter groups its similes with unusual thematic tightness around three character types: the fool, whom honor does not fit, the sluggard, paralyzed by his own excuses, and the gossip, whose words are fuel for strife, closing with the hidden malice of a deceitful heart.
section.thesis: Honor is as unfitting for a fool as snow in summer, the sluggard's excuses reveal a self-deceived paralysis, and without gossip a quarrel dies out, since hatred that hides behind smooth speech will finally be exposed before everyone.
section.frameNote: Four clusters: honor unfitting a fool, and the paradox of answering folly; the fool's mouth, the fool's honor, and the danger of hiring a fool; the sluggard's excuses and endless turning; the gossip who kindles strife, and the deceit that hides hatred.

verses.text: Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not befit a {{kesil|fool}}.
Like a fluttering sparrow or darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not come to rest.
A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the backs of fools!
Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him.
Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes.

units.label: The fool's mouth and honor
units.note: hiring a fool, honoring a fool

verses.text: Like cutting off one's own feet or drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool.
Like lame legs hanging limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool.
Like binding a stone into a sling is the giving of honor to a fool.
Like a thorn that falls into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of a fool.
Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby.
As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly.
Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.

units.label: The sluggard's excuses
units.note: the door turns on its hinges

verses.text: The slacker says, "A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!"
As a door turns on its hinges, so the slacker turns on his bed.
The slacker buries his hand in the dish; it wearies him to bring it back to his mouth.
The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly.
Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own.
Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows,
so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I was only joking!"
Without wood, a fire goes out; without {{ragan|gossip}}, a conflict ceases.
Like charcoal for embers and wood for fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.
The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being.
Like glaze covering an earthen vessel are burning lips and a wicked heart.
A hateful man disguises himself with his speech, but he lays up deceit in his heart.
When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart.
Though his hatred is concealed by deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.
He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who rolls a stone will have it roll back on him.
A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin.

kesil.gloss: Fool, the stubborn, self-satisfied person who resists correction. Verse 1 says honor fits him as poorly as snow fits summer, an image of things fundamentally out of season and out of place, capturing how deeply mismatched status and folly are.

ragan.gloss: Gossip, whisperer, one who stirs conflict through repeated talk. Verse 20 says a conflict ceases without this kind of talebearing, just as a fire dies without wood, showing gossip is not a passive habit but active fuel that keeps quarrels burning.

basic.context: This chapter is unusual for how tightly its similes cluster around three character types in turn: the fool, whom honor never fits and whose folly is as compulsive as a dog returning to its vomit, the sluggard, whose lion-in-the-road excuses hide sheer paralysis, and the gossip, whose fuel keeps every quarrel burning, and whose hidden hatred will one day be exposed before everyone.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter teaches almost entirely through vivid simile, and famously offers what looks like a direct contradiction, verses 4 and 5, do not answer a fool according to his folly, then answer a fool according to his folly. Read together rather than separately, they teach discernment: sometimes silence protects you from becoming like the fool, sometimes a pointed answer prevents the fool from imagining he has won, and wisdom knows which moment calls for which response.
basic.originalLanguages: Kesil, fool, verse 1, is pictured as someone honor fits as poorly as snow fits summer, capturing not stupidity so much as a fundamental mismatch of character and status. Nirgan, gossip or whisperer, verse 20, names one whose repeated talk is the literal fuel of conflict, so that removing this fuel, not merely staying silent about it, is what allows a quarrel to finally die.
basic.typology: The exposure of hidden hatred in the assembly, verse 26, anticipates the final judgment where all hidden things are brought to light, 1 Corinthians 4:5. The pit dug for another that swallows its own digger, verse 27, echoes the pattern fulfilled at the cross, where the schemes of Jesus' enemies became the very means of His victory over them.
basic.christ: Verse 26's promise that concealed hatred will finally be exposed in the assembly anticipates the New Testament's teaching that God will bring every hidden thing to light and disclose the purposes of the heart, 1 Corinthians 4:5, a judgment only Christ can execute justly because He alone sees hearts perfectly. And verse 27's image of a man falling into the pit he dug for another echoes, in miniature, the great reversal of the cross, where the very plot to destroy Jesus became, in God's hands, the means of defeating sin and death themselves.
basic.god: God's justice is patient but certain, since hidden hatred behind smooth speech, verse 26, will finally be exposed, and self-destructive schemes, digging pits and rolling stones meant for others, verse 27, tend to recoil on their authors even within this life. He gives wisdom the discernment to know when silence and when a pointed answer best serves truth, verses 4 to 5, rather than a single rule for every encounter with folly.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 4:5 echoes the exposure of hidden things promised in verse 26. Galatians 6:7 echoes the certainty of consequence in digging a pit for another, verse 27. Psalm 7:15-16 pictures the wicked falling into the very pit they dug, paralleling verse 27. James 3:5-6 develops the destructive fire imagery of gossip and the tongue in verses 20-21.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 26 exposes the fool who cannot be honored, the sluggard paralyzed by excuse, and the gossip whose fuel keeps quarrels alive and whose hidden hatred will one day be exposed. The whole story of Scripture answers with the promise that God will finally bring every hidden thing to light, and with Christ, whose enemies' own schemes became the means of their defeat and His victory.

context.literary:
Proverbs 26 is a gallery of portraits, hung in three rooms. The first room, verses 1 to 12, holds the fool, and the second, verses 13 to 16, the slacker. The third, verses 17 to 28, holds the quarreller, the gossip and the smooth talking hater. Each room opens with a cluster of similes and ends with a verse that turns the picture on the viewer: the fool's room ends with a man who is wise in his own eyes and has less hope than the fool, verse 12; the slacker's with a man wiser in his own eyes than seven who answer discreetly, verse 16. The phrase 'wise in his own eyes' joins the two rooms by a link that is easy to miss, and it shows that the chapter's real subject is self deception.

The chapter's form is as telling as its content. Almost every verse in the first half is built on 'like' or 'as,' with the comparison placed first and the person second, so the reader meets the image before the idea. In the second half the form changes to the parallel couplets of the sayings that describe cause and result: without wood a fire goes out, verse 20; he who digs a pit will fall into it, verse 27. The chapter thus moves from pictures that provoke the imagination to principles that govern consequence.

Verses 4 and 5 are a deliberate pair, placed side by side with almost identical wording and opposite commands, and they sit at the very centre of the first room. The editor who arranged them knew they would collide. The pairing is a lesson in how Proverbs wants to be read: not as a list of rules to be applied mechanically, but as a school of discernment.

The chapter ends with an enclosing theme of speech. The last verses move from the fool's mouth and the gossip's words to the flatterer and the liar, so the book returns to the tongue, which is where the portraits began, in verses 2, 7 and 9.
context.historical:
The images come from the working world of ancient Israel, and most would have been understood at once. Snow in summer and rain at harvest were out of season and harmful: rain at harvest in the dry months could spoil the crop on the threshing floor, as Samuel's sign of thunder and rain at wheat harvest shows, 1 Samuel 12:17 to 18. A whip, a bridle and a rod, verse 3, were the tools of animal handlers, applied to the fool as to beasts who do not respond to reason. A sling, verse 8, was a shepherd's weapon, and an archer who shoots at random, verse 10, was a danger to everyone nearby.

Public life supplies the setting for the chapter's warnings about messengers and employment. In a world without postal services, a message was carried by hand, and the messenger's reliability was the whole value of the message, verse 6. Hiring labour in the village meant taking whoever stood in the market, verse 10, and the proverb counts that as dangerous when the worker is unreliable.

The tavern and the village quarrel stand behind verses 17 to 22. A passer by who grabs a dog by the ears is meddling in the way a bystander might who steps into a feud between families. A gossip who passes on 'choice morsels' was a familiar figure in a community where honour and shame governed social life and a reputation could be made or lost on a rumour. The 'assembly' of verse 26 was the village gathering at the gate, where justice was done in public and a man's hatred could finally be exposed to his neighbours.

A dog in the ancient Near East was a scavenger, not a pet, so the image of a dog returning to its vomit, verse 11, was as unpleasant to the first hearers as it is to us. The pit and the stone of verse 27 correspond to the hunter's trap and the heavy rock rolled down a slope, and both are the sort of device that can turn on its maker.
context.canonical:
Several of the chapter's lines are cited or paralleled elsewhere. The dog and its vomit is quoted in 2 Peter 2:22 as a proverb true of false teachers who return to corruption after knowing the way. The motive of verse 12, being wise in one's own eyes, recurs in 3:7, 12:15 and 28:11, and in Isaiah's 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes,' Isaiah 5:21. Paul takes it up in Romans 1:22, 'Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools,' and in 1 Corinthians 3:18, where the way to wisdom is first to become a fool in the world's terms.

The slacker's lion is a repeat of 22:13, and the hand buried in the dish repeats 19:24. The words of the gossip in verse 22 are word for word the words of 18:8, so the book treats the gossip's morsels as a theme it will not let go. The pit that returns on its maker is the language of the Psalms, 'He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making,' Psalm 7:15, and of Ecclesiastes 10:8. The story of Haman, hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, Esther 7:10, is the narrative embodiment of the verse.

For speech that kills, James takes the image of fire and says the tongue is a fire, a world of wickedness that sets the course of life ablaze, James 3:5 to 6, which is a development of verses 20 and 21. The hidden hatred exposed in the assembly meets Jesus's promise that nothing concealed will not be disclosed, Luke 12:2 to 3, and Paul's statement that the Lord 'will bring to light what is hidden in darkness,' 1 Corinthians 4:5. The pair in verses 4 and 5 is lived out in the Gospels, where Jesus sometimes answers His questioners and sometimes declines, Luke 20:1 to 8, Mark 15:5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage's first aim was to teach discernment about people. A young man heading into the village, the court or the market would meet fools, idlers and gossips, and the chapter equips him to recognise them and respond. The warning is practical: do not honour a fool with a position, do not send him with a message, do not hire him by chance, because the damage is out of proportion to the cost. The collection of similes serves as a field guide.

The second aim is self scrutiny. The refrain 'wise in his own eyes' in verses 5, 12 and 16 turns the lens inward. The hearer is invited to feel superior to the fool and the slacker, and then discovers that the chapter's worst case is the person who cannot see that he is one of them. The sage wants his pupil to ask whether his own certainty is earned.

Third, the sage wants to protect community life. The quarrel, the whispered rumour and the 'I was only joking' of verse 19 are described as fire, not as small irritations, because they destroy the trust on which village life depends. The pupil is warned to starve the fire by refusing to be the wood.

Finally, the chapter assures the wise that the story is not left to the schemer. The hater who disguises his heart will be exposed, and the digger of pits will fall in. This is not a call to wait idly for vengeance but a basis for patience: the world is ordered so that deceit does not finally win, and the faithful need not meet it with its own methods.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is description, offered to train the eye. Calling someone a fool or a slacker is not meant to be a licence for contempt. The categories describe a set of tendencies seen in a person who refuses correction, and the book uses them to warn the reader, not to rank other people. Believers who take the portraits as a way to sort their neighbours into the wise and the foolish have missed the closing note of verse 12: the greatest danger is the man who is certain he is not a fool.

The commands that do appear, verses 4 and 5, are given as a pair and resist being read as a flat rule. That asks the reader for judgment in each case, the very thing the book exists to train. The promises of retribution, in verses 26 and 27, are likewise general statements about the moral order, not guarantees that every schemer will be caught in this life. Psalm 73 shows a faithful person wrestling with the cases where this does not appear to happen, and the answer there is the end of the story, not the next week.

The warnings against meddling and gossip carry straight over as moral obligations, since Scripture elsewhere forbids slander and calls for truthfulness, Ephesians 4:29. The caution about answering a fool carries over as wisdom: Paul tells Timothy to reject foolish speculation that breeds quarrels, and to be kind and forbearing, 2 Timothy 2:23 to 24. The believer is not told to despise the foolish, since Paul says that 'we too were foolish,' Titus 3:3.

debates.question: How can 26:4 and 26:5 both stand?

views.label: Different situations call for different responses
views.case: Some fools should be left unanswered because debate would drag you into their level, and others should be answered because silence would let them think they have won. The wise person reads the situation. This is the most common reading and fits the rest of the book's habit of presenting truths that must be balanced.

views.label: Different ways of answering
views.case: Another view distinguishes a manner of answer. Do not answer in the fool's spirit, with his insults and bluster, but answer with the substance that his folly needs to hear, in the way a wise person would. The same verb carries both senses, and the two verses speak to two sides of one act.

views.label: A deliberate paradox to teach discernment
views.case: Others argue that the editor placed the pair together on purpose so that the reader stops reading for rules and starts reading for wisdom. No rule settles which verse applies, so the reader must grow in the skill the book is trying to build.

debates.bearing: All three agree that wisdom lies in knowing the moment. Jesus shows it in practice: He sometimes silenced His questioners with a question, Luke 20:3 to 8, and sometimes made no further reply, Mark 15:5. The aim in either case is not to win but to avoid becoming like the fool and to prevent the fool from thinking his folly is wisdom.

debates.question: Can an undeserved curse really do harm, 26:2?

views.label: A causeless curse has no power
views.case: The proverb's picture is of a bird that flutters but never lands. A curse spoken without a cause finds no place to rest, because the moral order and God's justice do not back it. Balaam's attempt to curse Israel is the standing example, for the LORD turned the curse into a blessing, Deuteronomy 23:5.

views.label: A curse is only as strong as the cause behind it
views.case: Others note that the book assumes curses are powerful when they have a just cause, as the curse for moving a boundary stone, Deuteronomy 27:17, and that the proverb limits itself to the undeserved kind. The point is not that curses are empty but that they are tied to the truth.

debates.bearing: The two views agree on the practical lesson: a believer who has done no wrong need not be afraid of malice, since the LORD protects the one who trusts Him. The proverb gives no encouragement to use curses, and the New Testament calls believers to bless those who curse them, Luke 6:28.

study.originalLanguages:
Several Hebrew words in this chapter carry more than the English can show. The first is the word for the fool himself. In Proverbs the kesil is a moral figure more than an unintelligent one: he is the person who will not be taught, and his problem is a stubborn will, not a low intelligence. This is why 26:12 can say that there is more hope for a fool than for the man who is wise in his own eyes, because the fool at least has not yet closed the door of correction.

The second is the phrase translated 'wise in his own eyes,' in verses 5, 12 and 16. It appears also in 3:7 and 28:11, and in the prophet's woe, Isaiah 5:21. It describes a person who treats his own judgment as the final authority. The phrase is a reminder that what is at stake is not talent but trust: whom does he rely on?

Third, the laziness of verses 13 to 16 uses the slacker, atsel, from the earlier chapters. The excuse in verse 13 repeats 22:13, with a small variation: the lion is in the road, and then in the broad squares. The addition of a second place makes the excuse grow, as excuses tend to do. The hand in the dish in verse 15 repeats 19:24 with a milder verb, 'it wearies him.' The slacker's final trait in verse 16 is that he is wiser than seven who 'answer discreetly,' where the Hebrew word for discretion is ta'am, a word that literally means taste. A person with taste has a sense for what is fitting, and the sluggard has lost it.

Fourth, the 'joking' of verse 19. The man who deceives his neighbour and says 'I was only joking' uses the verb of play, sachaq. It is play with a firebrand. The wise man reads the damage, not the intention, and the proverb will not let a person hide behind a laugh.

Fifth, the gossip of verse 20, ragan, whose participle describes someone who spreads talk. The word is related to the verb for grumbling, and in 16:28 it is the one who separates close friends. Verse 22 is identical to 18:8, so the book offers the gossip's morsels twice. The image of verse 23 is notoriously difficult. The BSB footnote says the Hebrew reads 'burning' lips, and the ancient Greek reads 'smooth.' Many translators take the second word to be the dross of silver, the word used in 25:4, and picture a thin glaze that makes a clay pot look like silver. Either way the picture is of a surface that hides what is beneath. The verb for 'disguise' in verse 24 comes from the root of recognising, and means to make oneself unrecognisable.

typology.type: The wise silence and the wise reply, Proverbs 26:4 to 5
typology.fulfillment: The pairing of the two verses finds its human fulfilment in the Lord. Before Pilate 'Jesus made no further reply,' Mark 15:5, and before Herod He 'gave no answer,' Luke 23:9, in fulfilment of the servant who 'did not open His mouth,' Isaiah 53:7. Yet when the chief priests demanded His authority He answered with a question that exposed them, Luke 20:3 to 8. He is the perfect discerner of the moment. The correspondence goes further than skill. His silence was the silence of one who 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. The type falls short because the proverb trains wisdom in ordinary people, and Christ's judgment never errs.

typology.type: The pit that swallows its digger, Proverbs 26:27
typology.fulfillment: Haman built a gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it, Esther 7:10, and the nations fall into the pit they made, Psalm 9:15. The cross is the greatest reversal of the pattern. The rulers who killed the Lord of glory did not understand, 1 Corinthians 2:8; they carried out 'God's set plan,' Acts 2:23, and the death they devised became the means by which He disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:15. The escalation is that the trap sprung on the innocent One does not simply return on the trappers. It frees their captives. The type is partial: Haman's end was judgment alone, while the cross also offers mercy.

typology.type: The imagined lion and the real one, Proverbs 26:13
typology.fulfillment: The slacker invents a lion in the road as a reason to stay in bed. Scripture elsewhere names a real lion, 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David,' who 'has triumphed,' Revelation 5:5. The association is a contrast and not an allegory: the lion in the proverb is a pretext, while the Lion of Judah is a conqueror who has dealt with every fear that keeps His people still. The servant in the parable who buried his talent out of fear was called wicked and lazy, Matthew 25:25 to 26. The type falls short, because the proverb is a joke at the sluggard's expense and does not intend the Messiah.

typology.type: The smooth speech of hidden hatred, Proverbs 26:24 to 26
typology.fulfillment: The hater who speaks graciously while his heart is full of deceit finds a living example in those who came to Jesus with praise on their lips: 'Teacher, we know that You are honest,' Matthew 22:16, after they had conspired to trap Him, Matthew 22:15. Jesus saw through them, 'You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?' Matthew 22:18. The proverb promises that hidden hatred will be exposed in the assembly, and the Gospel shows it exposed by the One who sees the heart. The type falls short in that Jesus alone saw the heart perfectly, and the proverb advises ordinary believers to be wary, not omniscient.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through His own wisdom in answering. The proverb's pair of commands, answer not and answer, is lived out in the Gospels with a sureness no one else has had. He met the chief priests' challenge with a question that left them unable to reply, Luke 20:3 to 8. He met the Pharisees' flattering trap with a coin and a word that left them amazed, Matthew 22:15 to 22. And at His trial, 'He did not open His mouth,' Isaiah 53:7, so that Pilate was amazed, Mark 15:5. He did not retaliate when abused, 1 Peter 2:23. In each case He did what 26:4 and 26:5 aim at together: He neither became like the fool nor allowed the fool to think himself wise.

Second, the chapter's hardest verse, 26:12, finds its echo in Jesus's word to the Pharisees: 'If you were blind, you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains,' John 9:41. The proverb says there is more hope for a fool than for a man wise in his own eyes, and Jesus shows the same logic. The sinners and the little children came to Him, and the self assured went away. Paul takes this to its heart: 'the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing,' and 'the foolishness of God is wiser than man's wisdom,' 1 Corinthians 1:18 and 1:25. The way into His wisdom is to stop being wise in our own eyes, which is why Paul says one must become a fool to become wise, 1 Corinthians 3:18.

Third, the pit that swallows the digger comes to its highest form at the cross. The rulers of the age plotted and killed Him and thought they had won. But He was 'delivered up by God's set plan,' and God raised Him, 'because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' Acts 2:23 to 24. On the cross He 'made a public spectacle' of the powers, 'triumphing over them,' Colossians 2:15. The schemers' stone rolled back on them, and the stone rolled away from His tomb. The verse describes a general rule; the resurrection shows the rule at work in its greatest case.

Fourth, the chapter is a diagnosis of the tongue that Christ comes to heal. Jesus says that 'out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks,' Matthew 12:34, and He is the one on whose lips was found no deceit, 1 Peter 2:22. He calls Himself 'the truth,' John 14:6, over against the devil, the 'father of lies,' John 8:44. The liar who hates those he crushes, 26:28, has his opposite in the One who loves the people He lays down His life for. Those who were once foolish are then washed and renewed, Titus 3:3 to 5. A caution is in order: the fool, the slacker and the gossip are not Christ, and the chapter should not be pressed into allegory. The links come from the New Testament's own use of fool, wisdom and speech.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who built a moral world in which folly, idleness and malice carry their own consequences. The pit digger falls in; the fire without wood goes out; the one who rolls a stone has it roll back, verses 20 and 27. These are not signs of a mechanical universe but of the Creator's wisdom. The consequences are woven into the world He made, and yet He remains the Judge who exposes what is hidden, verse 26. The psalmist's words about the pit, Psalm 7:15 to 16 and Psalm 9:15, root the principle in His justice. He is patient, because the consequences take time, and He is certain, because they come.

The chapter also shows a God who opposes self deception. Those who are wise in their own eyes are the subject of the prophet's woe, Isaiah 5:21, and James gives the principle its widest form: 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble,' James 4:6. The proverb's stark verdict that a self assured man is a worse case than a fool is the doctrine of grace seen from the human side. If God gives His favour to the humble, then the first thing He asks is the honesty to see our own folly.

Third, the chapter shows God's hatred of lying and deceit. The flatterer, the smooth tongued hater, the man who deceives and says 'I was only joking,' all offend the God for whom truth is not an option. He is the one before whom nothing is concealed, Luke 12:2 to 3, and who judges the secrets of the heart, Romans 2:16. He holds people to account for careless words, Matthew 12:36. This is both terrifying and consoling. It is terrifying for the liar, and it is consoling for the one whose reputation has been crushed in the dark, because God sees what was said and why.

He is also a God of mercy toward fools. The chapter is hard on foolishness, but Paul tells Titus that 'we too were foolish,' and that God saved us 'not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy,' Titus 3:3 to 5. The same God who describes the fool so sharply is the one who made a way for the fool to be changed. The proverb diagnoses; the gospel heals.

In worship, the chapter leads to confession and to prayer. We ask to be saved from being wise in our own eyes, from the words that light fires, and from the excuses that keep us in bed. We also give thanks that He sees the hidden hatred we have suffered and will answer it, so that we need not repay it ourselves.

crossReferences.note: The father's early warning, 'Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil,' states positively what 26:12 and 26:16 describe in their ugliest form. Reading the two together shows that the fear of the LORD is the cure for the self assurance that chapter 26 holds up as the worst case.

Peter quotes the dog returning to its vomit, together with the saying about the washed sow, to describe false teachers who return to corruption after knowing the way of righteousness. It shows that 26:11 was read as a warning about relapse, and that an outward cleansing does not change the nature.

The prophet's woe on those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight repeats the language of 26:12. It shows the proverb's concern is not private only; a whole people can fall into the self assurance that refuses correction and then faces judgment.

This verse is word for word the same as 26:22, on the gossip's words like choice morsels. The book's repetition is intentional. It underlines how easy it is to swallow a rumour and how deeply it settles in the heart, so that the gossip's harm is done as much by the listener as by the speaker.

The psalmist describes the wicked man who digs a hole and falls into the pit of his own making, so that his violence falls on his own head. It is the poetic sibling of 26:27, and it grounds the proverb's principle in the LORD's justice.

Haman is hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. It is the clearest narrative example in Scripture of 26:27, and it also shows the proverb at work in public: the schemer's own device ends him while the one he plotted against is delivered.

James describes the tongue as a small spark that sets a forest ablaze, a fire set alight by hell. It develops 26:20 to 21, where a quarrel needs fuel to burn, and gives the New Testament weight to the warning that speech can destroy a community.

Jesus assures His disciples that nothing concealed will fail to be disclosed, and that what is whispered in the inner rooms will be shouted from the housetops. It is the New Testament counterpart of 26:26: hatred hidden behind smooth speech will be exposed.

When the chief priests demand His authority, Jesus answers with a question about John's baptism and then declines to answer theirs. It is a living instance of 26:4 and 26:5, showing the perfect Wise Man deciding when to answer a fool in a way that exposes, and when to refuse.

Paul says that anyone who thinks he is wise in this age must become a fool so that he may become wise. It is the gospel's answer to 26:12: the way out of being wise in your own eyes is to let go of that wisdom and receive the wisdom that comes from God.

study.oneStory:
This chapter belongs to the part of the Bible's story that deals with what the fall did to the human mind and mouth. In Eden the serpent's question led the first pair to become wise in their own eyes, to know good and evil on their own terms, Genesis 3:5. The fool, the slacker and the gossip of Proverbs 26 are descendants of that moment. Distrust of God's word became self trust, labour became toil and excuse, and speech became a means of accusation and deceit. The portraits are not a collection of oddities. They are the human condition after Genesis 3 seen at close range.

The story presses on to the problem of how such people can be changed. The law could describe the problem and the wisdom books could train the eye, but neither could make a fool wise. The prophets see this, and so Isaiah pronounces a woe on the clever and Jeremiah longs for a new heart. Israel's history reads like the chapter itself: the nation returns to its folly like a dog to its vomit, and the judgment that falls on it is the pit it dug for itself.

Christ enters this story as the wisdom of God and as the one who bears the folly of His people. The Wise Man who knows when to speak and when to be silent is led to the cross in silence, 'like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7. The pit dug for Him becomes the means of salvation, Acts 2:23 to 24, and the powers that plotted His death are shown up, Colossians 2:15. His people, who were once foolish, are washed and renewed, Titus 3:3 to 5, and are given a new mouth. Their speech is meant to build up and not to burn, Ephesians 4:29.

The end of the story is the place where the hidden is revealed and deceit is no more. Nothing impure enters the new Jerusalem, nor anyone who practises what is false, Revelation 21:27. The fire of the tongue is gone, and the gossips and the liars are outside, Revelation 22:15. The wise in their own eyes are replaced by people who see by the light of the Lamb. What the chapter could only picture, a mouth free of malice and a heart free of disguise, is what the redeemed will have.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 compare honor given to a fool to?

options.text: Snow in summer and rain at harvest, things fundamentally out of place.
options.note: Honor is pictured as deeply mismatched with a fool's character.

options.text: Apples of gold in silver settings.
options.note: That image, from 25:11, describes fitly spoken words, not honor given to a fool.

options.text: A well-timed and welcome gift.
options.note: The verse's point is mismatch and unfittingness, not welcome timing.

options.text: Rain during the normal rainy season.
options.note: The verse specifies rain at harvest time, when it is unwelcome and out of season, not during the normal rainy season.

quiz.q: How should the seeming tension between verses 4 and 5 be best understood?

options.text: As teaching discernment: different dangers call for either silence or a pointed answer.
options.note: Wisdom knows which response fits which situation rather than applying one rule always.

options.text: As a scribal error that should be corrected.
options.note: The text is intentional, not an error to be fixed.

options.text: As proof that Proverbs contains unreliable, contradictory teaching.
options.note: This misunderstands the genre and purpose of the juxtaposition.

options.text: As meaning you should always answer a fool according to his folly.
options.note: This ignores verse 4's equally valid warning against becoming like the fool through pointless argument.

quiz.q: According to verse 20, what happens to conflict without gossip?

options.text: It ceases, just as a fire goes out without wood.
options.note: Gossip is pictured as the active fuel that keeps quarrels burning.

options.text: It intensifies without gossip to distract from it.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's point.

options.text: It remains exactly the same regardless of gossip.
options.note: The verse specifically ties conflict's continuation to gossip's presence.

options.text: It slowly fades over a period of years.
options.note: The verse's image, a fire going out without wood, suggests a more immediate cessation, not a slow multi-year fade.

quiz.q: What does verse 24-25 warn about a hateful man's gracious speech?

options.text: Do not believe him, for he disguises his speech while laying up deceit in his heart.
options.note: Smooth, gracious words can mask genuine hatred and deception.

options.text: Gracious speech always reflects a truly changed heart.
options.note: This is exactly what the passage warns against assuming.

options.text: Gracious speech is a minor concern compared to actions.
options.note: The passage treats deceptive gracious speech as a serious matter in itself, not a minor one.

options.text: Gracious speech should be believed unless proven otherwise later.
options.note: The passage's counsel is immediate caution, 'do not believe him,' not a wait-and-see approach.

quiz.q: What does verse 27 say happens to one who digs a pit for another?

options.text: He will fall into it himself.
options.note: Schemes meant to harm others tend to recoil on their authors.

options.text: He successfully traps his intended victim every time.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the verse promises.

options.text: Nothing happens to him at all.
options.note: The verse specifically describes a consequence for the schemer.

options.text: He is only punished if caught by others.
options.note: The verse describes an inherent, near-automatic consequence, not one contingent on being caught.

questions: Verses 4 and 5 teach that wisdom sometimes calls for silence and sometimes for a direct answer. Think of a recent conflict with a foolish or stubborn person. Which response did you actually need, and which did you give?
The sluggard invents a lion in the road to avoid work, verse 13. What excuse are you currently using to avoid a responsibility you know you should face?
Verse 20 says a conflict dies without gossip to fuel it. Is there a quarrel or tension you have been unintentionally keeping alive through repeating what you have heard?
Verses 24-25 warn against trusting gracious words that mask a hateful heart. Have you ever been fooled by smooth speech, or have you used smooth speech to mask your own resentment?
Verse 27 promises that pits dug for others tend to swallow their diggers. Is there a scheme, grudge, or manipulation you are engaged in that this proverb should make you reconsider?

translationNotes.note: The juxtaposition of seemingly opposite commands is widely regarded as intentional, not contradictory, teaching that wise responses to folly depend on discerning the specific situation.
'Like binding a stone into a sling' pictures rendering a weapon useless or even dangerous to the user, since honoring a fool similarly misfires and can backfire on the one who grants it.

'Glaze covering an earthen vessel' pictures a cheap clay pot given an attractive silvery coating, an image of surface beauty hiding a common, even worthless interior, matching smooth speech over a wicked heart.
